# Diagnostic codes

<!-- type: reference · level: 1 -->

Every refusal nano-ros prints carries a code, `NROS-` and four digits:

```text
error[NROS-0004]: src/demo_bringup/system.toml: names no board
  help: add `board = "<board>"` to the `[image.<id>]` table in system.toml
  explain: nros explain NROS-0004
```

The `explain:` line is a command: `nros explain NROS-0004` prints the
code's section below without a network or a checkout. A code never
changes its meaning, and a retired code names the one that replaced it.

| Code | What went wrong |
| --- | --- |
| [NROS-0001](#NROS-0001) | ROS 2 is not sourced, and the project has messages to generate |
| [NROS-0002](#NROS-0002) | an image names a board that no board descriptor claims |
| [NROS-0003](#NROS-0003) | the workspace declares no image |
| [NROS-0004](#NROS-0004) | an image names no board |
| [NROS-0005](#NROS-0005) | a board's platform reaches no built-in family |
| [NROS-0006](#NROS-0006) | no diagnostic has this code |

<a id="NROS-0001"></a>

## NROS-0001: ROS 2 is not sourced, and the project has messages to generate

`nros configure`, `nros build` or `nros run` stopped before building anything,
because this shell has not sourced ROS 2 and the project has messages to
generate.

nano-ros generates every message type a project uses (a talker's `std_msgs`,
for example) from the message definitions of your ROS 2 install, so the types
and their hashes match your ROS 2 peers. It finds that install through
`AMENT_PREFIX_PATH`, which sourcing ROS 2 sets. A configure that ran in a
sourced shell records the prefix in the project, so later commands do not
need it; this project has no such record yet.

It happens on every board and every RMW, Linux and Cyclone DDS included.

### How to fix it

Source ROS 2 once, in this shell, and run the same command again:

```bash
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash   # or your overlay's install/setup.bash
nros build
```

That configure records the prefix in the project. Later builds and runs of
the same project reuse it, from any shell, an IDE or a CI step. A new project
records its own, so its first build needs a sourced shell again.

The refusal's `help` line, unless the site gives a more specific one:

> source ROS 2 in this shell (`source /opt/ros/<distro>/setup.bash`, or your overlay's `install/setup.bash`) and run the command again; later shells need not source it

<a id="NROS-0002"></a>

## NROS-0002: an image names a board that no board descriptor claims

An image names a board that no board descriptor claims, so nano-ros does not
know what to build it for.

`[image.<id>] board` in a bringup's `system.toml` is where an image names its
board. Each board crate ships a descriptor whose `names` list says which
spellings it answers to, and several are aliases for one board
(`mps2-an385-baremetal`, `baremetal` and `bare-metal` all name one
descriptor). A name that none of them lists is refused by name rather than
guessed at, because a guess builds the wrong image and reports success.

### How to fix it

Check the spelling in `system.toml`:

```toml
[image.demo]
board = "mps2-an385-freertos"
```

`nros board list` prints every board this SDK has. If the board is your own,
its board package must be on the board search path.

The refusal's `help` line, unless the site gives a more specific one:

> check the spelling of the image's `board`; `nros board list` names every board this SDK has

[Back to the list of codes](#diagnostic-codes)

<a id="NROS-0003"></a>

## NROS-0003: the workspace declares no image

`nros build` (or a verb that resolves images) found no `[image.<id>]` in any
bringup package of the workspace, so there is nothing to build.

An image is the buildable unit of nano-ros: one board, one RMW, and the
components that run on it. It is declared in a bringup package's
`system.toml` (a directory holding `package.xml` and `system.toml`, and no
code). A workspace whose bringup declares no image, or that has no bringup
package at all, has nothing for `nros build` to plan.

### How to fix it

Add an image to the bringup package's `system.toml`:

```toml
[image.demo]
board = "linux"
```

If the workspace has no bringup package yet, `nros new <ws> --board <board>
--template talker` shows the shape, and `nros configure --migrate` moves a
`system.toml` that sits beside a package's code into one.

The refusal's `help` line, unless the site gives a more specific one:

> add `[image.<id>] board = "<board>"` to the bringup package's system.toml

[Back to the list of codes](#diagnostic-codes)

<a id="NROS-0004"></a>

## NROS-0004: an image names no board

An `[image.<id>]` table in `system.toml` has no `board` key, so nano-ros does
not know what to build the image for.

Every image names exactly one board. The board decides the target triple, the
RTOS, the toolchain and the network setup; nothing else in the project can
stand in for it.

### How to fix it

Add the board to the image's table:

```toml
[image.demo]
board = "mps2-an385-freertos"
```

`nros board list` prints the boards this SDK has.

The refusal's `help` line, unless the site gives a more specific one:

> add `board = "<board>"` to the `[image.<id>]` table in system.toml

[Back to the list of codes](#diagnostic-codes)

<a id="NROS-0005"></a>

## NROS-0005: a board's platform reaches no built-in family

A board names a platform that is not one of nano-ros's built-in platforms, and
the platform's `inherits` chain does not reach one, so nano-ros does not know
which family's build rules the platform takes.

A platform you add yourself (`nros new platform`) is described by its
`nros-platform.toml`. Its `inherits` key names the built-in family it builds
like (`freertos`, `zephyr`, `bare-metal`, and so on), directly or through
another platform that does. The refusal names the chain it followed, and says
which of these went wrong:

- the chain ends at a platform that inherits nothing;
- a name in the chain is neither built in nor answered by any
  `nros-platform.toml` on the platform search path;
- the chain loops back on itself.

### How to fix it

Add `inherits` to the platform the refusal names, choosing the built-in family
it is closest to:

```toml
# nros-platform.toml
inherits = "freertos"
```

A platform that does not exist yet is scaffolded with
`nros new platform <name> --inherits <family>`.

The refusal's `help` line, unless the site gives a more specific one:

> add `inherits = "<family>"` to the platform's nros-platform.toml

<a id="NROS-0006"></a>

## NROS-0006: no diagnostic has this code

`nros explain` was given a code, spelled `NROS-` and four digits, that no
diagnostic has.

Every code nano-ros prints is compiled into the `nros` binary, so this one was
mistyped, or comes from a newer release than this binary. The refusal lists
the three codes nearest the one you gave.

### How to fix it

Copy the code from the `explain:` line of the refusal that printed it. If it
came from a newer nano-ros, run that release's `nros explain`.

A file that happens to be named like a code is reached as a path:
`nros explain ./NROS-0412`.

The refusal's `help` line, unless the site gives a more specific one:

> check the code against the refusal that printed it
